## Common Collocations
- **lavar los platos** — to wash the dishes; standard expression (not "limpiar los platos")
- **hacer la cama** — to make the bed; uses **hacer**, not "arreglar" or "limpiar"
- **poner la mesa** — to set the table; literally "to put the table"
- **pasar la aspiradora** — to vacuum; literally "to pass the vacuum cleaner"
- **sacar la basura** — to take out the trash
- **barrer el piso** — to sweep the floor
- **tender la ropa** — to hang the laundry; Latin America. Spain: **colgar la ropa**.
- **prender/apagar la luz** — to turn the light on/off; Latin America uses **prender**, Spain uses **encender**

## False Cognates and Tricky Translations
- **la habitación** vs **habit**: **Habitación** means "room," not "habit." A habit is **un hábito**.
- **la carpeta** vs **carpet**: **Carpeta** means "folder." Carpet is **la alfombra**.
- **la ropa** vs **rope**: **Ropa** means "clothing." Rope is **la cuerda**.
- **mover** vs **mudarse**: **Mover** means to physically move an object. To move to a new home is **mudarse** (reflexive). "I moved last year" = "Me mudé el año pasado," NOT "Moví el año pasado."

## Dialect Variations
- **bedroom**: **el dormitorio** (universal/formal), **la habitación** (Spain, widely understood), **la recámara** (Mexico)
- **stove/cooktop**: **la estufa** (Mexico, Central America), **la cocina** (Spain, South America — same word as "kitchen")
- **closet/wardrobe**: **el clóset** (Latin America, from English), **el armario** (Spain)
- **refrigerator**: **el refrigerador** (most of Latin America), **la nevera** (Spain, Colombia, Caribbean). Note gender change.
- **blanket**: **la cobija** (Mexico, Colombia), **la manta** (Spain), **la frazada** (Argentina, Peru)
- **living room**: **la sala** (Latin America), **el salón** (Spain), **el living** (Argentina, from English)
- **apartment**: **el departamento** (Mexico, Southern Cone), **el apartamento** (Caribbean, Central America), **el piso** (Spain)

## Cultural and Pragmatic Notes
- **Household chores as shared vocabulary**: In many Latin American families, discussing chores (quehaceres) is daily conversation. Knowing these verbs enables natural small talk.
- **Multi-generational homes**: Extended family living together is more common than in the US. "Vivimos con mis suegros" is not unusual and carries no stigma.
- **Diminutives for home items**: Mexicans frequently use diminutives: **casita** (little house, said affectionately), **cocincita**, **camita**. These express affection, not literal smallness.
- **Ser vs estar with the home**: **La casa es grande** (inherent quality). **La casa está limpia** (current state, result of effort). **La casa está en la esquina** (location). This cluster is ideal for reinforcing the ser/estar distinction.

## Pronunciation Alerts
- **almohada** — the **h** is silent: al-mo-A-da. Stress on third syllable.
- **sábana** — esdrújula (stress on SÁ): SÁ-ba-na. Without the accent, **sabana** means "savanna."
- **lámpara** — esdrújula: LÁM-pa-ra. English speakers tend to stress the second syllable.
- **jardín** — stress on the final syllable: jar-DÍN. Not JAR-din.
- **garaje** — the **j** is a Spanish /x/ (guttural h): ga-RA-je. Not a French "zh" sound.
- **llave** — the **ll** sounds like English "y" in most of Latin America (YA-ve), "sh" in Argentina.
